title: Energy: Where It Comes From, Where It Goes
subtitle: Why nothing is ever really used up
subject: Physics

p: Here is a strange idea. In the whole universe, energy is never made and never destroyed. Not once. Not by a volcano, a rocket, or a star. You can only move energy from one place to another, or change it from one kind into another. Physicists call this the conservation of energy, and in nearly 200 years of careful measuring, nobody has ever caught it being broken.

So why does your phone battery run flat? Why does a car need fuel? The energy did not vanish. It changed into forms that are harder to use, mostly warmth spread thinly into the air. Your phone is slightly warmer. The road behind the car is slightly warmer. The energy is still out there. It has just spread out.
This book follows energy from the Sun, through plants and wires and batteries, into your body, and out again. Nothing is lost. But a lot gets spread.
pages.cap: Energy flows from the hot cup into the room. The total never changes.
pages.fact: Did you know? The energy in a single raisin could lift you about 15 metres straight up, if your body could spend it all at once.

p: Energy comes in a handful of forms, and each one can turn into the others.

Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. A rolling ball, a falling raindrop, the wind: all kinetic. Double the speed and you get four times the energy. Potential energy is stored by position or shape: a book on a high shelf, a stretched elastic band, water behind a dam. Chemical energy is stored in the bonds between atoms, in food, wood, gasoline and batteries. Thermal energy is heat: the jiggling of atoms themselves. Electrical energy is carried by moving electrons. Light and radio waves carry radiant energy. And nuclear energy sits inside the centre of atoms, locked up tighter than anything else.
A pendulum shows the swap. At the top of its swing it is all potential energy. At the bottom it is all kinetic. In between, it is trading one for the other, over and over.
pages.cap: At the top: stored energy. At the bottom: motion. The total stays the same.

pages.h: Energy changes form. It never disappears.
p: A rock falls, a wire glows, a plant grows, a car brakes. Every one is the same energy, wearing a new costume.

pages.h: Where does a ball's energy go?
p: Roll a ball down a ramp and across a floor. It slows down and stops. If energy is never destroyed, where did the ball's energy go?

Into heat. As the ball rubs against the floor and pushes through the air, friction turns its motion into tiny vibrations of atoms in the ball, the floor and the air. The floor is warmer by a few millionths of a degree. You cannot feel it, but a sensitive thermometer could.

This happens to almost all motion on Earth. Bike brakes get hot. Meteors glow white at 1,600 degrees Celsius as air friction eats their speed. Space probes keep going for decades because there is almost nothing to rub against: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is still moving at 17 kilometres per second, more than 25 billion kilometres away, using no fuel at all.
On Earth, motion always leaks into heat. In space, it mostly does not.
pages.cap: The ball keeps rolling, but friction is slowly turning its motion into warmth.

p: Scientists measure energy in joules, named after James Joule, who in the 1840s showed that stirring water makes it warmer. One joule is about the energy it takes to lift an apple one metre. Small. So we use bigger units.

A kilojoule is 1,000 joules. Food labels in Canada show both kilojoules and calories; one food calorie is about 4.2 kilojoules. A banana holds about 400 kilojoules, enough to lift that apple 400 kilometres, or to run your body for about an hour.

Power is different from energy. Power is how fast energy moves, measured in watts: one joule every second. A phone charger uses about 20 watts. A kettle uses 1,500. A kilowatt-hour, the unit on electricity bills, is 1,000 watts flowing for one hour: 3.6 million joules. It costs about 10 to 20 cents in most of Canada.
Your body, sitting still, runs at roughly 100 watts. You are a warm, thinking light bulb.
pages.cap: A kettle draws fifteen times more power than your resting body.

pages.q: A ball rolls across a floor and stops. Where did its energy go?
opts: It became heat in the floor, the ball and the air
It went back up the ramp
pages.why: Friction turns motion into tiny vibrations of atoms, which is heat. The total amount of energy is unchanged.

p: Everything is made of atoms, and atoms never sit still. They vibrate, bounce and spin. Heat is simply this jiggling. The faster the atoms move, the hotter the thing is. Temperature is a measure of the average energy of that motion.

This explains why there is a lowest possible temperature. If you slow atoms down and down, eventually they are barely moving at all. That point is absolute zero: minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. Nothing can be colder, because there is no motion left to take away. Laboratories have come within a billionth of a degree of it, but never reached it.

It also explains why heat flows from hot to cold and never the other way on its own. Fast atoms bump slow ones and share their energy, the way a crowd of running children spreads out through a quiet room. Hold an ice cube and the heat flows from your hand into the ice, not from the ice into you. Cold is not a thing. It is just less heat.
pages.cap: Solid, liquid, gas: the same molecules, jiggling harder as they warm.

pages.h: Why spread-out energy is tired energy
p: If energy is never destroyed, why can't we collect all the warmth in the air and run a city on it? There is plenty of it. The problem is not the amount. It is how spread out it is.

Useful energy is concentrated: a tank of fuel, a charged battery, water high behind a dam. When you use it, it spreads into billions of tiny atom-jiggles in the air and ground. Gathering it back up would cost more energy than you would get. Physicists have a word for how spread out energy is: entropy. In every real process, entropy goes up. That is the second law of thermodynamics, and it has no known exceptions.

So energy is never used up, but it does get 'tired'. The universe is slowly turning concentrated energy into lukewarm nothing-much. Every engine, every living thing, every star is riding that one-way flow. That is why you need fresh food, fresh fuel and fresh sunlight.
pages.cap: Far in the future, stars burn out and energy is spread too thin to use. That is entropy winning.

pages.h: Try it: make heat with your hands
p: Turn motion into heat and feel it happen.
steps: Press your palms together and rub them hard and fast for 20 seconds. Feel the warmth: that is kinetic energy becoming heat through friction.
Hold a thick elastic band against your upper lip, which is sensitive to temperature. Stretch it quickly and hold it. It feels warm.
Keep it stretched for 10 seconds, then let it relax quickly against your lip. It feels cool. The band took energy from your lip to pull its molecules back into their tangled shape.
Bend a paper clip back and forth 20 times, then touch the bend. Warm again. Where did that heat come from?
pages.cap: Every rub, stretch and bend turns muscle energy into warmth.
pages.safe: Rub gently enough that your skin does not get sore.

pages.h: Almost everything starts with the Sun
p: The Sun is a ball of hydrogen so heavy that its own gravity crushes the centre to 15 million degrees Celsius. There, hydrogen atoms fuse into helium, and a little mass turns into a lot of energy. Every second, the Sun converts about 4 million tonnes of matter into light. It has done this for 4.6 billion years and will keep going for about 5 billion more.

The light made in the core bounces between particles for tens of thousands of years before it finally reaches the surface. Then it takes just 8 minutes and 20 seconds to cross 150 million kilometres to Earth.

Earth catches about 173,000 terawatts of sunlight: that is 173 million billion watts, roughly 10,000 times more than all of humanity uses. Most of it warms the ground and sea, drives the wind and lifts water into clouds. A tiny slice gets caught by leaves. That slice feeds nearly everything alive.
pages.cap: Fusion in the core: every second, 4 million tonnes of the Sun become light.

p: A leaf is a machine for catching sunlight and storing it as chemical energy. Inside, green chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light. The plant uses that energy to pull carbon dioxide out of the air and water out of the ground, and bolt them together into sugar. Oxygen is the leftover. This is photosynthesis.

Plants are not very efficient: most crops store only 1 to 2 percent of the sunlight that lands on them. But there are so many plants that, together, they capture about 130 terawatts, six times what all human machines use.

Everything you eat is stored sunlight. The grass holds it, the cow eats the grass, and you eat the cow or drink the milk. At each step, about 90 percent is spent on living and lost as heat, which is why there are far more grass plants than cows, and far more cows than wolves. When you run, you are burning sunlight that fell on a field last summer.
pages.cap: Sun to grass to rabbit to fox. At each step, nine-tenths of the energy escapes as heat.

p: Coal, oil and natural gas are the remains of plants and tiny sea creatures that lived mostly 100 to 350 million years ago. They captured sunlight, died, were buried, and were cooked and squeezed for ages until only energy-rich carbon was left. When you burn them, you are releasing sunlight that fell before the dinosaurs.

They are concentrated, cheap to dig up and easy to move, which is why the world still gets about 80 percent of its energy from them. A single litre of gasoline holds 34 megajoules, as much energy as your body uses in about three days.

The catch is what else comes out. Burning fossil fuels puts the ancient carbon back into the air as carbon dioxide, about 37 billion tonnes a year. That gas traps heat, and the planet is warming. The energy was never the problem. The leftover gas is. That is why so much work now goes into getting energy from sources that do not burn.
pages.cap: Burning: carbon joins oxygen, heat and light come out, carbon dioxide goes into the air.

pages.q: Where did the energy in a litre of gasoline originally come from?
opts: Sunlight caught by living things millions of years ago
pages.why: Fossil fuels are buried plants and plankton that stored sunlight long before the dinosaurs.

pages.h: How a power station makes electricity
p: In 1831, Michael Faraday moved a magnet near a coil of copper wire and saw a current flow. That one trick still makes almost all the world's electricity. Spin a magnet inside coils of wire, and electrons in the wire are pushed along. The spinning machine is called a generator.

The hard part is the spinning. In most power stations, fuel boils water into steam at over 500 degrees Celsius, the steam blasts through a turbine, and the turbine spins the generator. Coal, gas and nuclear plants all work this way; they just heat the water differently. Hydro dams skip the steam and let falling water spin the turbine. Wind turbines let the wind do it.

So electricity is not a source of energy. It is a way of moving energy from somewhere a magnet is spinning to somewhere you want a light on. A big generator can push out 1,000 megawatts, enough for about a million homes.
pages.cap: Steam spins the turbine, the turbine spins the generator, the generator pushes electrons.

pages.h: The grid: a machine the size of a country
p: Electricity leaves a power station through wires at very high voltage, up to 765,000 volts, because high voltage loses less energy as heat along the way. Near your town, transformers step it down to 240 volts for homes. The whole web of wires, towers and transformers is the grid.

The grid has a strange rule: supply must equal demand every single second. Electricity cannot pile up in the wires. If everyone turns on a kettle at once, operators have to spin up more generators within seconds, or the frequency drops and things start to fail. Control rooms watch this 24 hours a day.

Canada makes about 60 percent of its electricity from falling water, one of the cleanest grids in the world. Quebec, Manitoba and British Columbia are almost all hydro. Alberta and Saskatchewan still get most of theirs by burning gas and coal. The push in the wires travels at close to the speed of light, so a lamp lights the instant you flip the switch.
pages.cap: A night skyline is the grid at work: thousands of generators balanced to the second.

p: Here is an uncomfortable number. A coal power station turns only about 35 to 40 percent of the coal's energy into electricity. The rest leaves as hot gas up the chimney and warm water into a river. A car engine is worse: about 25 percent of the gasoline moves the car, and 75 percent heats the air.

Then there is the light bulb. An old-fashioned incandescent bulb turns 5 percent of its electricity into light and 95 percent into heat, which is why it burns your fingers. An LED bulb gives the same light for about one-tenth the power, so a 60-watt bulb is now a 7-watt bulb. Switching bulbs is one of the easiest ways to save energy that exists.
None of this energy is destroyed. All of it is spread into the surroundings as heat. Efficiency is about how much useful work you squeeze out before that happens.
pages.cap: A glowing filament: mostly a tiny heater that happens to make some light.

pages.h: Your body runs on about 100 watts: the power of an old light bulb.
p: Resting, you turn food into heat at 100 joules every second. Sprinting, you briefly hit 1,000 watts, more than a microwave oven.

A solar panel has no moving parts. It is made of thin slices of silicon with a tiny amount of other elements added. When a particle of light, a photon, hits the silicon, it knocks an electron loose. The panel is built so that loose electrons can only leave one way, through a wire. That one-way flow is electricity, straight from sunlight.

Ordinary panels turn about 20 to 23 percent of sunlight into electricity. The best laboratory cells pass 45 percent. A typical rooftop panel, about 2 square metres, makes around 400 watts in full sun.

The big story is price. Since 2010, the cost of a solar panel has fallen by about 90 percent. In 2024 the world installed more than 500 gigawatts of solar, more than any other kind of power station, and solar is now the cheapest new electricity in most sunny countries. The problem is the obvious one: at night, nothing. That is where storage comes in.
pages.cap: A photon knocks an electron loose from a silicon atom; the panel sends it down a wire.

p: Wind is solar energy too. The Sun heats the ground unevenly, warm air rises, cooler air rushes in, and the air moves. A wind turbine catches that motion with blades shaped like aeroplane wings. The blades spin a shaft, the shaft spins a generator.

Modern turbines are enormous. The newest offshore machines stand 260 metres tall with blades over 120 metres long, and each one can make 15 megawatts, enough for about 15,000 homes. Bigger is better because wind is steadier and stronger higher up.

There is a surprising rule hidden in the wind. The power you can catch goes up with the cube of the wind speed. Double the wind, and you get eight times the power. That is why turbines are built on hills, coasts and out at sea, and why a calm day gives almost nothing. Like solar, wind needs partners: other sources, long wires to windier places, and batteries.
pages.cap: A turbine blade is a wing. Air flowing over it pulls the blade round.

pages.h: Water and the heat inside the Earth
p: Falling water is the oldest big source of electricity and still the largest renewable one. A dam holds water high up, which is potential energy; let it drop through a turbine and it becomes electricity. China's Three Gorges Dam makes up to 22,500 megawatts, the most powerful power station on Earth. Canada's largest, the Robert-Bourassa station in northern Quebec, makes about 5,600 megawatts.
Hydro is also solar: the Sun lifts the water into the sky, and rain puts it back behind the dam.

One energy source is not from the Sun at all. The inside of the Earth is hot: about 5,000 degrees Celsius at the core. Some of that is leftover heat from the planet's formation, and some comes from radioactive atoms slowly breaking down in the rock. About 47 terawatts leaks out through the surface. Iceland and New Zealand drill into hot rock and use the steam to make electricity and heat homes.
pages.cap: The Earth leaks 47 terawatts of ancient heat. Volcanoes are where it bursts out.

pages.q: Which of these does NOT get its energy from the Sun?
pages.why: Earth's inner heat comes from radioactive atoms and the planet's formation. Wind, rain and buried plants all start with sunlight.

pages.h: Nuclear: energy from the centre of the atom
p: Inside every atom is a nucleus, and inside some heavy nuclei, like uranium, is the most concentrated energy we know how to use. Hit a uranium-235 nucleus with a neutron and it splits, releasing heat and more neutrons, which split more atoms. This is fission. The heat boils water, and the rest is a normal power station.

The numbers are astonishing. One kilogram of uranium-235, if every atom split, would release as much energy as about 3 million kilograms of coal. Albert Einstein's equation, E = mc squared, says why: a small loss of mass becomes an enormous amount of energy. Nuclear plants make about 9 percent of the world's electricity, and 15 percent of Canada's, mostly in Ontario, without making carbon dioxide.

The catch is the used fuel, which stays dangerously radioactive for thousands of years. Fusion, the Sun's method of joining atoms, would make far less waste. A giant test reactor called ITER is being built in France, but no fusion plant has yet powered a single home.
pages.cap: A nucleus the size of a dot, holding more energy than a truckload of coal.

p: A battery does not store electricity. It stores chemical energy and turns it into electricity on demand. Inside are two different materials and a liquid or paste between them. One material wants to give up electrons, the other wants to take them. Connect a wire, and electrons flow through it from one side to the other. That flow is the current that runs your phone.
Charging runs the chemistry backwards, pushing electrons home so it can happen again. A lithium-ion battery can do this roughly 1,000 times before it wears out.

Batteries are heavy for what they hold. The best lithium-ion packs store about 250 watt-hours per kilogram. Gasoline stores about 12,000, almost 50 times more. That is why an electric car needs a 400-kilogram battery and why long-haul aeroplanes still burn fuel. Even so, battery prices have fallen about 90 percent since 2010, and a phone battery holds about 15 watt-hours: enough to lift you to the top of a 100-metre tower.
pages.cap: Electrons leave one side of the battery, do work in the bulb, and return to the other.

p: Batteries are not the only way to save energy for later. The oldest and biggest is pumped hydro. When electricity is cheap, pump water up to a high reservoir. When it is needed, let it fall back through turbines. About 90 percent of all the stored electricity on Earth sits in lakes like this.

Other ideas are being tested. Giant flywheels spin at 50,000 turns a minute in a vacuum and give back their motion in seconds. Towers of molten salt at 560 degrees Celsius hold heat from solar mirrors into the night. Compressed air is squeezed into old salt caves. Spare electricity can split water into hydrogen, which can be burned or run through a fuel cell later, though more than half the energy is lost on the round trip.
The hardest problem is seasons. Canada has sun in summer and cold in winter. Nobody has yet found a cheap way to store July's sunshine for January.
pages.cap: Lifting a weight stores energy; letting it fall gives it back. Pumped hydro does this with lakes.

p: Turn chemical energy into electricity with fruit.
steps: Push a galvanized (zinc-coated) nail into a lemon, and a copper coin or a strip of bare copper wire into the same lemon, about 2 centimetres apart and not touching.
Touch both metals with the two legs of a small LED. One lemon makes about 0.9 volts, which is not enough. Nothing lights yet.
Make three more lemon cells and connect them in a chain with short wires: the copper of one to the zinc of the next. Four lemons give about 3.5 volts.
Touch the free copper to the LED's long leg and the free zinc to the short leg. A faint glow. The zinc is slowly dissolving; its chemical energy is now light.
pages.cap: Zinc gives up electrons, copper collects them, the lemon juice carries the charge between.
pages.safe: Do not eat the lemons afterwards, and wash your hands when you are done.

p: Energy can also travel as light and other waves. Lightning is the loudest example on Earth. Inside a storm cloud, ice crystals and hailstones crash together and rub electrons off each other. The top of the cloud becomes positive, the bottom negative. When the difference reaches about 100 million volts, the air itself breaks down and a channel of current rips to the ground.

A single bolt carries around 1 billion joules and heats the air to 30,000 degrees Celsius, five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. The air expands so fast that it makes a shock wave: thunder. Light reaches you instantly; sound takes about 3 seconds per kilometre, which is how you can count the distance.

Could we catch lightning? Not really. A billion joules sounds huge, but it is only about 280 kilowatt-hours, what a Canadian home uses in ten days, delivered in a few millionths of a second to a place you cannot predict.
pages.cap: 100 million volts, 30,000 degrees, one billion joules, gone in a flash.

p: An average Canadian household uses about 10,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity a year, and in most of the country, more than that again in gas or oil for heat. Heating is the biggest single use, because winter is long. Hot water is next, then fridges, lights and screens.

The cleverest machine in a modern home is a heat pump. It does not make heat; it moves it. Even air at minus 20 degrees Celsius has heat in it, because its atoms are still jiggling. The pump squeezes that heat out of the outdoor air and pushes it inside, using about one unit of electricity to move three units of heat. A furnace that burns fuel can never beat one unit in, one unit out. A heat pump run backwards is an air conditioner.
Phantom power matters too. Chargers, consoles and TVs on standby can quietly use 5 to 10 percent of a home's electricity while doing nothing.
pages.cap: A heat pump moves warmth from the cold outdoors to the warm indoors: three joules moved for every one spent.

pages.q: A heat pump uses 1 unit of electricity and delivers 3 units of heat to a house. Where do the extra 2 units come from?
opts: They are created inside the pump
They are moved in from the outside air
From the wires in the wall
pages.why: Even cold air holds heat energy. The pump moves it indoors instead of making it, so energy is still conserved.

pages.h: Where the extra heat is going
p: Earth has an energy budget. Sunlight comes in, and the planet sends heat back out to space as invisible infrared light. For thousands of years the two balanced. Now they do not, quite. Carbon dioxide and methane from burning fuels let sunlight in but slow the heat getting out. The imbalance is small, about 1 watt on every square metre, but Earth has 510 trillion square metres.

Where is that extra energy going? More than 90 percent is going into the ocean, which is why sea water is warming. The rest melts ice and warms the air and land. The planet's surface is now about 1.3 degrees Celsius warmer than in the 1800s, and 2024 was the hottest year ever recorded.

This is the conservation of energy on a planetary scale. Trap a little more each year, and it has to show up somewhere. Scientists disagree on exactly how fast the warming will continue, but not on where the heat is coming from.
pages.cap: Earth at night: every light is energy spreading out, and some of it is being trapped.

p: The plan most countries are following has two parts: make electricity without burning anything, then run as much as possible on that electricity, including cars, heating and factories. Solar and wind are now the cheapest power in history, so the first part is moving fast. In 2025 the world got about 40 percent of its electricity from sources that make no carbon dioxide.
The second part is harder. Steel, cement and long flights need enormous, concentrated energy, and nobody has fully solved them. Storage for weeks at a time is still expensive.

Some things are honestly unknown. Will fusion ever be cheap enough to matter? Will new battery chemistries like sodium or solid-state take over? Can the grid be rebuilt fast enough? Engineers are testing all of these right now. Whatever the answer, the rule you learned on page one will hold: no energy is ever made or lost. We are only learning better ways to borrow it.
pages.cap: Two centuries of learning to borrow energy in new ways.

p: Here is where the simple rule gets strange. Astronomers measuring distant exploding stars in 1998 found that the universe is not just expanding; the expansion is speeding up. Something is pushing space apart. Nobody knows what. Scientists call it dark energy, which is really a name for 'we do not know'.

Measurements suggest that about 68 percent of everything in the universe is this dark energy, 27 percent is invisible dark matter, and only 5 percent is the atoms that make stars, planets and you. In 2024 and 2025, a telescope survey called DESI found hints that dark energy may be weakening over time. If that holds up, the textbooks will change. It is not yet certain.

Dark energy also complicates conservation of energy. In an expanding universe, the usual rule bends: light stretches and loses energy as it crosses space, and physicists still argue about where that energy goes. Even the firmest law in physics has edges where it gets fuzzy.
pages.cap: The oldest light in the universe, stretched by 13.8 billion years of expanding space.

pages.h: Every joule you use today has been travelling since the Big Bang.
p: It has been starlight, rock, rain, sugar and wire. For a moment it is you. Then it moves on.
